question: What is the proper mode of baptism in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and what is its purpose?
choices: Immersion in water by one holding proper priesthood authority, for the remission of sins
Sprinkling or pouring of water as an outward sign of an inward grace already received
A symbolic public declaration of faith with no saving efficacy of its own
Immersion that automatically saves the person regardless of repentance or authority
notes: Tests whether the model knows baptism is by immersion, by authority, for remission of sins — covenant ordinance, not mere symbol (Protestant view) nor mechanically saving. Distinguishes LDS ordinance theology from grace-symbol framings.

question: In confirmation, after baptism, how is the gift of the Holy Ghost conferred?
choices: By the laying on of hands by those holding the Melchizedek Priesthood
By the laying on of hands by an Aaronic Priesthood priest, as in baptism
Automatically at the moment of baptism, with no separate ordinance required
By the recipient's silent prayer accepting the Spirit into their heart
notes: Tests the priesthood distinction: a priest can baptize but confirmation/gift of the Holy Ghost requires Melchizedek authority. The near-miss conflates the two priesthoods; the 'automatic' option mirrors a Protestant view that baptism alone conveys the Spirit.

question: What do the bread and water of the sacrament represent, and what do members do as they partake?
choices: They are emblems representing Christ's body and blood; partaking renews baptismal covenants
They literally become Christ's body and blood, which members consume for grace
They are a memorial only, conveying no covenant and renewing no commitment
They represent the Holy Ghost, whose companionship members receive anew
notes: Tests understanding that the emblems are symbolic (not transubstantiation) AND covenant-renewing (not bare memorial). Two distinct traps bracket the correct nuance; the fourth confuses sacrament with confirmation.

question: What is the doctrinal basis for performing baptisms for the dead in temples?
choices: The deceased may accept or reject the vicarious ordinance in the spirit world, preserving agency
The ritual guarantees the deceased's exaltation regardless of their response
It retroactively makes the dead members of the Church without their knowledge or consent
It is a purely symbolic family ceremony with no claimed effect on the deceased
source: 1 Corinthians 15:29; D&C 128; Gospel Topics, Baptisms for the Dead
notes: Tests grasp of agency: vicarious ordinances offer, not impose, salvation. The anti-Mormon framing ('making the dead members without consent') and the deterministic folk view are common distortions corrected by official teaching.

question: Which list correctly gives offices in the Aaronic Priesthood?
choices: Deacon, teacher, priest, and bishop
Deacon, teacher, elder, and priest
Priest, elder, high priest, and bishop
Deacon, teacher, priest, and seventy
notes: Tests whether the model can separate Aaronic offices (deacon, teacher, priest, bishop) from Melchizedek offices (elder, high priest, seventy, apostle, patriarch). Each distractor smuggles in a Melchizedek office.

question: What is the difference between a priesthood office and priesthood keys?
choices: An office is an authority to act in a calling; keys are the right to direct the use of the priesthood
Keys and office mean the same thing; every ordained man holds keys
Keys are physical temple keys; an office is merely a title of respect
An office gives a man keys automatically, so every elder holds keys to lead the Church
source: D&C 107; General Handbook 3.4.1; Boyd K. Packer, 'The Power of the Priesthood'
notes: Tests the keys-vs-office distinction: ordination confers an office, but keys (the right to preside/direct) are conferred separately and held by specific leaders. Distractors collapse the distinction in several common ways.

question: In Latter-day Saint theology, what is a covenant?
choices: A two-way promise between God and a person, with conditions set by God
A one-sided gift from God requiring nothing of the recipient
A contract between two members enforced by the bishop
A personal resolution one makes to oneself to live better
notes: Tests covenant theology: a reciprocal, conditional promise with God ('I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say'). The one-sided-gift option reflects a grace-alone framing; the others reduce covenant to a horizontal contract or private goal.

question: What does the temple sealing ordinance accomplish for a husband, wife, and their children?
choices: It can bind them as a family for time and all eternity, conditional on faithfulness
It guarantees the family will be together eternally no matter how they later live
It seals them only for this mortal life, ending the relationship at death
It is a beautiful tradition with no claimed effect beyond the wedding day
notes: Tests that sealing blessings are real but conditioned on faithfulness — not unconditional (folk assurance) nor merely 'till death do you part' (the very thing sealing transcends). Distinguishes covenant sealing from civil marriage.

question: Which best describes what the temple recommend interview is meant to certify?
choices: A member's worthiness — their faith in Christ and obedience to covenants — to enter the temple
That a member has paid a fee granting access to the temple
That a member has achieved sinless perfection before entering
That a member's family has held Church membership for a required number of generations
source: General Handbook 26.3; temple recommend interview questions (rev. Oct 2019)
notes: Tests that the recommend assesses worthiness/faithfulness — not payment, not sinless perfection, not pedigree. The 'fee' option is a hostile distortion; the perfection and lineage options are common misunderstandings of the worthiness standard.
